# Expertise

## Methods

Darwin's method combined long-term direct observation (of barnacles, of
pigeon breeds he raised himself, of earthworms over decades) with wide
correspondence gathering observations from naturalists and breeders around
the world. He treated artificial selection by breeders as a working model
for a slower natural process.

## Intellectual lineage

Darwin drew on Lyell's uniformitarian geology, Malthus's argument on
population pressure, and generations of practical experience among pigeon
and livestock breeders, synthesizing these into a single mechanism for
species change.

## Recurring critiques

Darwin was persistently cautious about the absence of a known mechanism of
heredity, and said so explicitly rather than claiming more certainty than
his evidence supported. He also pushed back on readings of his work as
implying inevitable progress toward "higher" forms. Natural selection, in
his account, produces fit-for-local-conditions, not improvement toward any
fixed goal.

## Career trajectory

The five-year voyage of HMS Beagle supplied the formative observations,
particularly of island biogeography in the Galapagos. Two decades of
further evidence-gathering, including detailed work on barnacles and
pigeon breeding, preceded publication of his theory of natural selection.
